title: Intelligence Hawks Plot to Sneak Through Warrantless Spying
excerpt: They want to use the National Defense Authorization Act to extend a program that expired in June, even though the new Democratic majority would likely reform it.
content_html:
Intelligence hawks are once again posturing to help the Trump administration reauthorize its warrantless surveillance program, even as the outlook for privacy reforms has been boosted considerably by midterm victories in the House and Senate. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico the strategy: reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which expired in June, by attaching it to the typically must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) before the lame-duck session comes to an end.

Democratic intelligence hawks have kept their cards close on whether they would support using the NDAA as a vehicle to renew the surveillance authority in the lame duck, but history suggests those hawks would be hard-pressed to miss the opportunity. In fact, Democratic supporters of Section 702 see the midterm triumph for their party as a bad development for their priorities.

Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), currently ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the intelligence community’s strongest ally in Congress, knows that a clean reauthorization of Section 702 would be unlikely to pass after the lame-duck session. Himes, who is in line to chair the Intelligence Committee next year, told The Hill as much in an interview last week, arguing that Congress needs to “get this thing done in the lame duck because … it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”

Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) have also backed a lame-duck FISA extension. (Kelly also serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee.)

According to Elizabeth Goitein, co-director of the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, Himes and other Democratic intelligence hawks “are out of step with the rest of their caucus, and with the rest of Congress.” As the Prospect reported earlier this year, reclaiming the majority is one way to force fair votes on privacy reform, namely warrant requirements for any spying on Americans. “I don’t see a world in which Democratic leaders do not allow votes on reforms, no matter who the Democratic leaders are [in the next Congress],” Goitein said.

That’s why Democrats like Himes and Warner want to get Section 702 through now. But the opposition to a clean extension has proven to be increasingly transpartisan. And privacy advocates across the country and on Capitol Hill are gearing up for a year-end fight to stop the warrantless spying agenda in its tracks.

“Using must-pass legislation like the NDAA to yet again try to force a clean reauthorization of this powerful tool is a desperate move to advance a warrantless surveillance agenda that has been rejected by the majority of Americans,” Amanda Beckham, government relations director at Free Press Action, said in a statement.

FREE PRESS ACTION IS PART of a coalition of several dozen civil society groups seeking to thwart intelligence hawks’ efforts to extend Section 702 in the lame-duck session. That coalition, which includes Demand Progress, the Brennan Center for Justice, and many more, warned against renewing the government’s surveillance authority in letters to congressional leadership last week.

Currently, the NDAA is in a House-Senate conference committee, even though Democrats blocked a floor vote in the Senate in July. Negotiators are getting pressure from intelligence hawks to add FISA Section 702 to the final conference report, which should emerge in the coming weeks.

“Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process,” coalition member organizations wrote in a November 12 letter. The following day, they sent a second letter, this time to Democratic leadership. Mother Jones was the first to report that in it, the coalition laid out an anti-surveillance agenda for Democrats to prioritize in the next Congress, calling on them to “make protecting Americans’ privacy and reining in surveillance an urgent congressional priority.”

The NDAA has passed every year since 1961, an unparalleled streak for a Congress that doesn’t get much of anything done on time. My colleague Robert Kuttner observed earlier this month, however, that there has been “more than trivial Republican opposition” to this year’s NDAA. Some Democrats want to remove a provision that they say would intertwine the U.S. and Israeli militaries, while the $1.5 trillion price tag President Trump has set has brought opposition. Yet the NDAA always manages to pass, and usually other measures that members of Congress want to quietly advance hitch a ride on the defense bill.

If Himes is to be believed, Section 702 is the nation’s “most rigorously overseen” intelligence program, which he claims is not prone to abuse. Privacy advocates roll their eyes at that last line, as the FBI shuttered an office responsible for monitoring Section 702 abuses last year, and has been notoriously noncompliant with the existing yet limited guardrails for protecting Americans’ privacy.

While there is broad bipartisan support for reforms like warrant requirements, members of Congress had no opportunity to vote on those reforms this year. “The only reason we didn’t have votes in this Congress was because the Trump administration made sure of it, and Speaker Johnson was obviously carrying the administration’s water on that,” Goitein said. But Republicans could never get a majority for a clean reauthorization either, and the warrantless spying measure expired.

Republican opponents of privacy reform have begun to manufacture a false sense of urgency around Section 702. One particularly glaring example was the op-ed Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) co-authored for The Wall Street Journal last week, “A Vital National Security Tool Shouldn’t Go Dark.” Cornyn and his co-author, Strauss Center Director Adam Klein, argue that failing to renew Section 702 in the lame-duck session “is risky” because intelligence officials may not have enough time to “seek new court orders before the current ones expire.” The reality is that since the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) certified Section 702 through mid-March of next year, intelligence officials have ample time to file for new certifications.

“The moment that the government files an application for new certifications, that filing extends the existing certifications until the FISA court has the chance to rule,” Goitein said.

To avoid an actual lapse, the government would simply need to file an application before March 17, 2027, making that roughly the deadline for Congress to renew Section 702. Moreover, if the government does need more time, Congress can temporarily extend the existing certifications for a brief period.

The intelligence community itself has continued to deploy scare tactics in a bid to secure Congress’s blessing for a clean extension of the surveillance authority.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe sent a letter to congressional leaders last week, warning that any delay in reauthorizing Section 702 would put “the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk in the heightened threat environment.” They attributed that heightened threat environment to Iran, which intelligence officials reportedly claimed has plans to target senior members of the Trump administration, with either a dirty bomb or chemical weapons attack in Washington, D.C.

But some intelligence officials cast doubt on whether Iran could feasibly execute such a sophisticated act of terror in the U.S., and the White House asserted that at this time, “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Critics also drew comparisons between the alleged bomb plot and the U.S. invasion of Iraq.

HIMES TALKS A BIG GAME when it comes to his role in overseeing the intelligence community. Now that Democrats will enjoy majority control in both chambers come January, he’s been talking an even bigger one. Himes himself is expected to lead the House Intelligence Committee in the next Congress.

In an interview with The New York Times last week, Himes revealed plans to probe the expansion of the CIA’s “extremely aggressive” covert operations under the Trump administration, while opening investigations into defense and intelligence contractors over their donations to the president’s vanity projects.

But Democrats can do much more with their oversight power in the next Congress. The obvious start is to add warrant requirements to Section 702 as a condition for continuing the program. That is likely to have support from a bipartisan majority next year.

But more can be done. For instance, the Offices of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) and U.S. Attorney General are required to submit semiannual reports to Congress on compliance with the statutory and constitutional requirements of Section 702.

“In the past, when these reports have been submitted,” Goitein said, “they’ve also been made public.”

The 29th Joint Assessment, which is the most recently declassified semiannual compliance report, was released in July 2025. According to an April 2026 staff report from the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board, the DNI and the attorney general have submitted Joint Assessments 30 through 33, none of which have been declassified. It also remains unclear whether the 34th and 35th Joint Assessments have been submitted by the DNI and the attorney general.

Another ripe area for intelligence community oversight in the next Congress is the failure of the DNI and the attorney general to declassify FISC’s March 2026 opinion by the statutory deadline on September 13. That opinion, in which the judge reportedly found serious issues with the filtering tools U.S. intelligence agencies use to sift through queries for information on individuals who have communicated with foreign intelligence targets, likely contains important information about how Section 702 is being run and could give a boost to reformers who want to fix the system. Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) have pressed the Trump administration for “flagrantly” violating the law.

What’s more, Wyden believes there are “credible allegations” that Clayton provided false testimony at his Senate confirmation hearing about the since-withdrawn subpoenas of New York Times journalists, which Clayton issued in the waning days of his tenure as the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.

“I think more broadly across authorities,” said Goitein, “Congress should be looking into how the administration has used and abused its surveillance powers.”

Ramming through a clean extension of Section 702 in the lame duck would be an abdication of the duty Congress has to openly debate an issue as consequential as Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, privacy advocates say.

“If and when this gets brought to a vote in the next Congress, if Congressman Himes wants to make the case to his caucus for why Trump should have warrantless access to Americans’ communications, that’s his right,” Goitein told the Prospect. “Let’s have that debate.”

content_html_zh:
Intelligence hawks are once again posturing to help the Trump administration reauthorize its warrantless surveillance program, even as the outlook for privacy reforms has been boosted considerably by midterm victories in the House and Senate. 它是。 Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politico the strategy: reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which expired in June, by attaching it to the typically must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) before the lame-duck session comes to an end.

Democratic intelligence hawks have kept their cards close on whether they would support using the NDAA as a vehicle to renew the surveillance authority in the lame duck, but history suggests those hawks would be hard-pressed to miss the opportunity. In fact, Democratic supporters of Section 702 see the midterm triumph for their party as a bad development for their priorities.

代表。 Jim Himes (D-CT), currently ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the intelligence community’s strongest ally in Congress, knows that a clean reauthorization of Section 702 would be unlikely to pass after the lame-duck session. Himes, who is in line to chair the Intelligence Committee next year, told The Hill as much in an interview last week, arguing that Congress needs to “get this thing done in the lame duck because … it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”

它是。 Mark Warner (D-VA), vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) have also backed a lame-duck FISA extension. (Kelly also serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee.)

According to Elizabeth Goitein, co-director of the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, Himes and other Democratic intelligence hawks “are out of step with the rest of their caucus, and with the rest of Congress.” As the Prospect reported earlier this year, reclaiming the majority is one way to force fair votes on privacy reform, namely warrant requirements for any spying on Americans. “I don’t see a world in which Democratic leaders do not allow votes on reforms, no matter who the Democratic leaders are [in the next Congress],” Goitein said.

That’s why Democrats like Himes and Warner want to get Section 702 through now. But the opposition to a clean extension has proven to be increasingly transpartisan. And privacy advocates across the country and on Capitol Hill are gearing up for a year-end fight to stop the warrantless spying agenda in its tracks.

“Using must-pass legislation like the NDAA to yet again try to force a clean reauthorization of this powerful tool is a desperate move to advance a warrantless surveillance agenda that has been rejected by the majority of Americans,” Amanda Beckham, government relations director at Free Press Action, said in a statement.

FREE PRESS ACTION IS PART of a coalition of several dozen civil society groups seeking to thwart intelligence hawks’ efforts to extend Section 702 in the lame-duck session. That coalition, which includes Demand Progress, the Brennan Center for Justice, and many more, warned against renewing the government’s surveillance authority in letters to congressional leadership last week.

Currently, the NDAA is in a House-Senate conference committee, even though Democrats blocked a floor vote in the Senate in July. Negotiators are getting pressure from intelligence hawks to add FISA Section 702 to the final conference report, which should emerge in the coming weeks.

“Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process,” coalition member organizations wrote in a November 12 letter. The following day, they sent a second letter, this time to Democratic leadership. Mother Jones was the first to report that in it, the coalition laid out an anti-surveillance agenda for Democrats to prioritize in the next Congress, calling on them to “make protecting Americans’ privacy and reining in surveillance an urgent congressional priority.”

The NDAA has passed every year since 1961, an unparalleled streak for a Congress that doesn’t get much of anything done on time. My colleague Robert Kuttner observed earlier this month, however, that there has been “more than trivial Republican opposition” to this year’s NDAA. Some Democrats want to remove a provision that they say would intertwine the U.S. and Israeli militaries, while the $1.5 trillion price tag President Trump has set has brought opposition. Yet the NDAA always manages to pass, and usually other measures that members of Congress want to quietly advance hitch a ride on the defense bill.

If Himes is to be believed, Section 702 is the nation’s “most rigorously overseen” intelligence program, which he claims is not prone to abuse. Privacy advocates roll their eyes at that last line, as the FBI shuttered an office responsible for monitoring Section 702 abuses last year, and has been notoriously noncompliant with the existing yet limited guardrails for protecting Americans’ privacy.

While there is broad bipartisan support for reforms like warrant requirements, members of Congress had no opportunity to vote on those reforms this year. “The only reason we didn’t have votes in this Congress was because the Trump administration made sure of it, and Speaker Johnson was obviously carrying the administration’s water on that,” Goitein said. But Republicans could never get a majority for a clean reauthorization either, and the warrantless spying measure expired.

Republican opponents of privacy reform have begun to manufacture a false sense of urgency around Section 702. One particularly glaring example was the op-ed Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) co-authored for The Wall Street Journal last week, “A Vital National Security Tool Shouldn’t Go Dark.” Cornyn and his co-author, Strauss Center Director Adam Klein, argue that failing to renew Section 702 in the lame-duck session “is risky” because intelligence officials may not have enough time to “seek new court orders before the current ones expire.” The reality is that since the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) certified Section 702 through mid-March of next year, intelligence officials have ample time to file for new certifications.

“The moment that the government files an application for new certifications, that filing extends the existing certifications until the FISA court has the chance to rule,” Goitein said.

To avoid an actual lapse, the government would simply need to file an application before March 17, 2027, making that roughly the deadline for Congress to renew Section 702. Moreover, if the government does need more time, Congress can temporarily extend the existing certifications for a brief period.

The intelligence community itself has continued to deploy scare tactics in a bid to secure Congress’s blessing for a clean extension of the surveillance authority.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe sent a letter to congressional leaders last week, warning that any delay in reauthorizing Section 702 would put “the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk in the heightened threat environment.” They attributed that heightened threat environment to Iran, which intelligence officials reportedly claimed has plans to target senior members of the Trump administration, with either a dirty bomb or chemical weapons attack in Washington, D.C.

But some intelligence officials cast doubt on whether Iran could feasibly execute such a sophisticated act of terror in the U.S., and the White House asserted that at this time, “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Critics also drew comparisons between the alleged bomb plot and the U.S. invasion of Iraq.

HIMES TALKS A BIG GAME when it comes to his role in overseeing the intelligence community. Now that Democrats will enjoy majority control in both chambers come January, he’s been talking an even bigger one. Himes himself is expected to lead the House Intelligence Committee in the next Congress.

In an interview with The New York Times last week, Himes revealed plans to probe the expansion of the CIA’s “extremely aggressive” covert operations under the Trump administration, while opening investigations into defense and intelligence contractors over their donations to the president’s vanity projects.

But Democrats can do much more with their oversight power in the next Congress. The obvious start is to add warrant requirements to Section 702 as a condition for continuing the program. That is likely to have support from a bipartisan majority next year.

But more can be done. For instance, the Offices of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) and U.S. Attorney General are required to submit semiannual reports to Congress on compliance with the statutory and constitutional requirements of Section 702.

“In the past, when these reports have been submitted,” Goitein said, “they’ve also been made public.”

The 29th Joint Assessment, which is the most recently declassified semiannual compliance report, was released in July 2025. According to an April 2026 staff report from the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board, the DNI and the attorney general have submitted Joint Assessments 30 through 33, none of which have been declassified. It also remains unclear whether the 34th and 35th Joint Assessments have been submitted by the DNI and the attorney general.

Another ripe area for intelligence community oversight in the next Congress is the failure of the DNI and the attorney general to declassify FISC’s March 2026 opinion by the statutory deadline on September 13. That opinion, in which the judge reportedly found serious issues with the filtering tools U.S. intelligence agencies use to sift through queries for information on individuals who have communicated with foreign intelligence targets, likely contains important information about how Section 702 is being run and could give a boost to reformers who want to fix the system. Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) have pressed the Trump administration for “flagrantly” violating the law.

What’s more, Wyden believes there are “credible allegations” that Clayton provided false testimony at his Senate confirmation hearing about the since-withdrawn subpoenas of New York Times journalists, which Clayton issued in the waning days of his tenure as the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.

“I think more broadly across authorities,” said Goitein, “Congress should be looking into how the administration has used and abused its surveillance powers.”

Ramming through a clean extension of Section 702 in the lame duck would be an abdication of the duty Congress has to openly debate an issue as consequential as Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, privacy advocates say.

“If and when this gets brought to a vote in the next Congress, if Congressman Himes wants to make the case to his caucus for why Trump should have warrantless access to Americans’ communications, that’s his right,” Goitein told the Prospect. “Let’s have that debate.”
